verses.text: For all this I laid to my heart, even to explore all this: that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; whether it is love or hatred, man doesn’t know it; all is before them.

All things come alike to all. There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked; to the good, to the clean, to the unclean, to him who sacrifices, and to him who doesn’t sacrifice. As is the good, so is the sinner; he who takes an oath, as he who fears an oath.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that there is one event to all: yes also, the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
For to him who is joined with all the living there is hope; for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
For the living know that they will die, but the dead don’t know anything, neither do they have any more a reward; for their memory is forgotten.
Also their love, their hatred, and their envy has perished long ago; neither have they any more a portion forever in anything that is done under the sun.
Go your way — eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
Let your garments be always white, and don’t let your head lack oil.

Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your life of vanity, which he has given you under the sun, all your days of vanity: for that is your portion in life, and in your labor in which you labor under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol,  where you are going.

I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favor to men of skill; but time and chance happen to them all.

For man also doesn’t know his time. As the fish that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare, even so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falls suddenly on them.
I have also seen wisdom under the sun in this way, and it seemed great to me.
There was a little city, and few men within it; and a great king came against it, besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it.
Now a poor wise man was found in it, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man.
Then I said, “Wisdom is better than strength.” Nevertheless the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.
The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him who rules among fools.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war; but one sinner destroys much good.

footnotes.content: The Teacher has been turning things over in his heart—what's the use of it all? He sees that the righteous, the wise, and their works all rest in God's hands. But we mortals cannot read His heart to know when He means love or when He means testing. It keeps us humble before Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This hits hard: good fortune and misfortune come alike to the righteous and the wicked. The clean and unclean meet the same fate. The oath-keeper and the oath-breaker face the same end. The Teacher is naming the mystery we all feel—that earthly goodness does not guarantee earthly safety. Yet God sees what we do not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This leveling is evil under the sun, he says—one fate for all, and it leaves the human heart twisted with madness. Knowing we must die, we grow wild with grasping and schemes. But the Teacher names this not as God's failure but as our blindness. He means to wake us to what truly matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A living dog is better than a dead lion—a strange comfort, but it is one. So long as we draw breath, there is hope. The Teacher is not despising the lion or praising the dog, but pointing to breath itself as a mercy. While we live, we can still turn, repent, and seek the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The living know they must die; the dead know nothing more. No reward comes to them; their name fades. The Teacher is not speaking of the afterlife in Jesus's light—he speaks from before the Cross. Yet even here, he guards us: remember that this earthly forgetting is not the final word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their love, hatred, envy—all have perished. They have no portion anymore in anything done under the sun. The Teacher strips away illusion: when we cling to earthly ties as if they are forever, we court despair. But a heart fixed on the eternal does not despair in losing the temporal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Go, eat your bread with joy. Drink your wine with a merry heart. God has already accepted your works. This is not mere pleasure-seeking; it is trust. The Teacher is saying: God has made His grace known; now receive it. Receive the gifts of His hand without anxiety, for His yes has already been spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: White garments and oil on the head—signs of joy and proper care in ancient custom. The Teacher calls us to live as if today is a day of feast, not perpetual mourning. In Christ, we learn that sorrow is real, but it is not the final note. We can dress in hope because we know the resurrection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Live joyfully with the wife you love. All your days of vanity are still your portion, your labor under the sun. The Teacher is not calling marriage vanity in itself, but earthly life as we know it. To cherish the spouse God has given you while you both draw breath—this is to hold your portion wisely and tenderly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might. In Sheol, the grave, there is no work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom. The Teacher calls us not to despair but to urgency and wholehearted labor in this life. We have now; we will not always. Let us work as for the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The swift do not always win the race; the strong do not always take the battle. Bread does not go to the wise, riches not to the understanding, favor not to the skilled. Time and chance fall upon all alike. The Teacher is breaking our illusions of control. All we can truly do is trust the One who holds time itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Man does not know his time. Like fish caught in an evil net or birds snared, we are suddenly trapped by an evil time we did not foresee. The Teacher is not mocking us but sobering us: we are smaller than we think. This is why we need a God larger than our lives—and we have one in Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Teacher returns to something he has seen: an example of wisdom that seemed great to him. He is about to tell a story—a little parable—to show us something that might otherwise escape our notice. Even in the vanity of this world, there are moments when wisdom shines.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A small city, few people, a great king besieging it with mighty bulwarks—a concrete story. The Teacher is not giving us history but a type, a picture of impossible odds. The city is helpless; power towers over it. Into this comes wisdom, which the world forgets.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A poor wise man is found in the city, and by his wisdom he delivers it. The city is saved. Yet no one remembers him. The Teacher shows us a hard truth: the world does not always see or honor the one who saves it. How much more reason, then, to do good not for fame but for God's eyes alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wisdom is better than strength, the Teacher declares. Yet the poor man's wisdom is despised; his words are not heard. He speaks the truth that could save, but the world closes its ears. We see this in Christ: the greatest wisdom came clothed in poverty and was rejected. Yet His word endures forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The quiet words of the wise are better heard than the loud shout of a fool who rules. The Teacher prizes depth over volume, truth over noise. In a world of endless shouting, stillness and true speech shine. This is a comfort: the Lord listens to the whispered prayer more than the world hears the loudest voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wisdom is better than weapons; one sinner destroys much good. Readers today hear an echo in these words—how one act of deception, one choice to betray, can unravel what wisdom has built. Yet we also see how one act of faithfulness, one choice to speak truth, can heal what was broken. As of 2026-10, we know the final wisdom: love overcomes all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
